title: The Safavids and Shah Abbas's Isfahan

cards.h: The empire that made Persia Shia
cards.b:
In 1501 a young leader named Ismail took the city of Tabriz and founded the Safavid dynasty. Over the next two centuries the Safavids turned Iran into a Shia state and a great centre of art and trade.

The Safavids fought the Ottomans and traded with Europe. Their story shows how religion and politics shaped the modern map of the Middle East.

Ismail claimed descent from a Sufi leader, Safi al-Din. He made Twelver Shia Islam the state religion, which was a major break with the Sunni Ottomans and most of their neighbours. Shia scholars were brought in from Arab lands to teach the new faith.

Iran's modern identity as a Shia country began with these decisions. They shaped every later ruler's relations with the Ottoman and Mughal worlds.

In 1514 the Ottoman sultan Selim I defeated Ismail at the battle of Chaldiran. The Ottomans had firearms and cannon, and the Safavid cavalry charged into them. Tabriz fell, and Ismail never fully recovered his power.

The battle taught the Safavids the value of guns. Later shahs built up their own artillery and recruited troops from the Caucasus. The Ottoman border would be fought over for generations.

Shah Abbas I (ruled 1588–1629)

Abbas rebuilt the army. He recruited Georgian, Circassian and Armenian soldiers who were loyal to the shah rather than to tribal leaders. He also reformed taxes and trade, and encouraged silk exports.

Persian chroniclers praised him as a great builder. Historians now see him as a ruler who balanced religion, trade and warfare with great skill.
The Safavids ruled for about two centuries. Their power faded in the 1700s, but their cultural legacy lasted far longer.

Abbas moved his capital to Isfahan. There he built the great square called Naqsh-e Jahan, flanked by the Shah Mosque, a royal palace and a bazaar. The square was one of the largest in the world at its time.

Persians have a proverb, "Isfahan is half the world." Travellers from Europe and India praised the gardens, bridges and tiled domes. Isfahan became a model of Persian urban life.

cards.h: Did Abbas force the Armenians to Isfahan?
cards.b:
A common story says that Shah Abbas forcibly moved thousands of Armenians from Julfa, near the border, to a new quarter called New Julfa in Isfahan. The story is often told as a tale of cruelty or of royal generosity.

Historians argue about how much was forced and how much was voluntary. Armenian merchants became key players in the silk trade. The community grew rich and kept its church and language in the city.

Silk was the great export of the Safavid empire. Persian raw silk was bought by Dutch and English merchants, who paid in silver. Abbas used the English to help take the island of Hormuz from the Portuguese in 1622.

The Persian Gulf became a battleground of trade. Silk, silver and spices flowed across it, and the rivalry of European companies changed how the Safavids made their deals.

Safavid painters created miniatures of great delicacy. Persian poetry, from Hafiz and Saadi, was read at court and copied in books that were treasured across Asia. The Persian language was the language of learning and government.

Historians argue whether Safavid culture was a continuation of earlier Persian traditions or a fresh start. The answer is probably both. The Safavid court gave new life to old forms.

Persian was the language of the Mughal court in India. Many of the empire's poets, painters and officials came from Iran. Mughal rulers looked to Safavid Persia for culture and model kingship.

In 1543 the Mughal emperor Humayun took refuge at the Safavid court. When he returned to India, he brought Persian painters with him. Their work helped shape the Mughal painting style that followed.

Five things to remember
  1. Ismail founded the Safavid dynasty in 1501.
  2. Chaldiran (1514) was lost to the Ottomans.
  3. Shah Abbas I moved the capital to Isfahan.
  4. Silk paid for Persian power.
  5. The Safavids made Shia Islam the state religion.
Think about it
  • Why did religion matter so much to state building?
  • How did firearms change the balance between Persia and the Ottomans?
